**Partly from memory, and I haven't verified any of this against the source.**

**What I'm fairly confident of:**
- The `paymentterms` table has `daysbeforedue` and `dayinfollowingmonth`. If `daysbeforedue > 0`, the term is "N days after invoice". Otherwise `dayinfollowingmonth` is used as a day-of-month.
- The overdue/aged queries branch on this in SQL, roughly:

```sql
CASE WHEN paymentterms.daysbeforedue > 0 THEN
    CASE WHEN TO_DAYS(Now()) - TO_DAYS(debtortrans.trandate) >= paymentterms.daysbeforedue
         THEN debtortrans.balance ELSE 0 END
ELSE
    CASE WHEN TO_DAYS(Now()) - TO_DAYS(
         DATE_ADD(DATE_ADD(debtortrans.trandate, INTERVAL 1 MONTH),
                  INTERVAL (paymentterms.dayinfollowingmonth - DAYOFMONTH(debtortrans.trandate)) DAY)
         ) >= 0
         THEN debtortrans.balance ELSE 0 END
END
```

So the due date is the transaction date plus one month, shifted to day `dayinfollowingmonth` of that month. The Overdue1/Overdue2 buckets add the 30/60-day offsets to the same expression.

**Which files use it:** I believe `CustomerInquiry.php` and `AgedDebtors.php` (plus the customer balance code in `includes/` and `SelectCustomer.php`) use this pattern. I'm not certain of the exact file list.

**Whether every script computes it identically:** I don't know. I can't recall whether every script uses the same expression. Some scripts may use different expressions or buckets, or compute it in PHP instead of SQL. I don't want to guess at discrepancies.

If you have a webERP checkout, point me at it. A `grep -rn dayinfollowingmonth` would settle both questions quickly.
